scatter.t: Each point is one house: **size across, price up**. We want one number that says whether the two variables **move together**, and in which direction.

positive.t: Bigger houses cost more: as size grows, price grows. The points climb from lower left to upper right. This is **positive covariance**.

negative.h: NEGATIVE: ONE UP, THE OTHER DOWN
negative.t: Now imagine price falls as size grows (say, size versus distance to the city). The points slide from upper left to lower right. This is **negative covariance**.

near-zero.t: Here the points show **no consistent upward or downward trend**. Knowing the size tells you nothing about which side of the average the price is on. Covariance is about zero.

covariance.t: Mark the means (the cross). Each point makes a **rectangle**: its distance from the mean in x times its distance in y. Green rectangles (same side of both means) count positive, red negative. Covariance is their average: **(6+2+0+1+8)/5 = 3.4**.

rescale.t: Measure size in units **ten times larger**. The points have exactly the same shape, yet covariance jumps from **3.4 to 34**. A raw covariance is hard to compare across variables.

correlation.t: Divide by both standard deviations: **Corr = Cov / (σx × σy) = 3.4 / (√2 × √6) ≈ 0.98.** Correlation is always between **−1 and +1**: +1 a perfect rising line, −1 a perfect falling line, 0 no straight-line trend.

zero-not-independence.t: These points follow **y = (x − 3)²**: y is completely determined by x. Yet the left and right halves cancel, so covariance and correlation are exactly **0**. Correlation only detects **straight-line** relationships.

ml-connection.t: **Highly correlated features are redundant.** Collect all the variances and covariances into a **covariance matrix**: it is the key ingredient of PCA and of the multivariate normal in the next checkpoint.
